screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn what iSCSI provides and why administrators use it. iSCSI delivers block-level storage over ordinary IP networks, allowing a remote LUN to behave like a locally attached disk. That matters because many server workloads — databases, virtual machine disks, and clustered filesystems — require raw block access for performance and control. We will focus on the Linux tooling: LIO as the kernel target framework and targetcli to build backstores, targets, portals, LUNs, and ACLs. You will also learn how to configure an initiator with iscsiadm, how CHAP authentication protects access, and what network and storage choices influence performance. A short lab demonstrates creating a 2 gigabyte logical volume, exporting it from a target, discovering and logging in from an initiator, then partitioning, formatting, and mounting the discovered disk. Common troubleshooting steps such as checking firewalls, verifying the target service, and testing basic TCP connectivity are included so you can diagnose discovery failures quickly. By the end you should understand when to choose iSCSI over file protocols and how to build a basic, secure iSCSI pair in Linux.

screens.title: What is iSCSI and why use it?
screens.narratorSegment: iSCSI is a protocol that exposes block storage over TCP/IP so a remote device appears as a local disk. That distinction — block versus file access — is critical. With file protocols like NFS, the client operates at the file level and the server's filesystem mediates input and output. With iSCSI, the initiator receives a raw block device and can partition, format, and manage filesystems directly. This direct access benefits workloads that depend on predictable block semantics and performance, such as databases and virtual machine disks, because there is no intermediate server filesystem layer handling each file operation. A concrete example: a hypervisor connecting a VM disk to centralized storage can mount the LUN and use its own filesystem optimizations and caching, often improving throughput and enabling features like multipathing. A common misconception is that iSCSI is simply "remote storage like NFS"; in reality it provides lower-level control and different failure modes — for instance, filesystem corruption can occur if two initiators write to the same block device without clustering. The takeaway is to choose iSCSI when you need raw block semantics and ensure your architecture accounts for exclusive access or clustering solutions when sharing LUNs between hosts.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › What is iSCSI and why use it?
Definition

iSCSI as block storage

iSCSI exposes remote storage over TCP/IP so the initiator sees a block device. This allows partitioning, formatting, and direct filesystem management from the client.

  • Use when applications need raw disk semantics and predictable I/O.
  • Common for VM disk stores, databases, and clusters that require block access.
  • Different failure and sharing considerations compared to file protocols.
Analogy

Think of NFS as a remote file cabinet where you request specific files. iSCSI is like plugging a remote hard drive into your machine; you control its partitions and filesystem directly.

Key Takeaway

Choose iSCSI when you need block-level control and be careful about co-mounting without clustering.

Concrete example

Hypervisor VM disk on iSCSI LUN

A hypervisor can present a VM's virtual disk as a file on NFS, or attach an iSCSI LUN as a raw device. With iSCSI the hypervisor controls the filesystem and can use multipathing and SAN-level snapshots, often improving performance for intensive VM I/O workloads.

Misconception
iSCSI is not automatically safer; it needs CHAP and network isolation to prevent unauthorized block access.
Why it matters
Block access provides control and performance but increases responsibility for access control and backup strategies.

screens.title: iSCSI components: Target, Initiator, IQN, LUN, TPG
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the components and their relationships prevents configuration mistakes. The iSCSI target is the server that exports storage; it uses backstores to represent the physical or logical devices that will be presented. The initiator is the client that connects and consumes a LUN as a block device. IQNs — iSCSI Qualified Names — uniquely identify targets and initiators and are used in ACLs. A LUN, or Logical Unit Number, maps a backstore to the target so it is presented to an initiator. A TPG, or Target Portal Group, defines the network interfaces and ports where the target listens; a portal ties a target to an IP and port combination, typically TCP 3260. For example, you might expose an LVM Logical Volume as a backstore, create a target with an IQN, add a portal binding to 192.168.1.100:3260, then create a LUN that maps the LV so that an initiator with a permitted IQN can attach. A common error is mismatched IQNs in ACLs or forgetting to create the portal on the correct interface. The core idea is that backstores become LUNs, which targets expose through portals and protect with ACLs identified by IQN.

keyIdea.title: Component mapping
keyIdea.text: Backstore → LUN → Target (IQN) → Portal/TPG → Initiator (IQN) with ACLs controlling access.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › iSCSI components
Architecture

How components relate

Each backstore is a real storage object: a file, block device, or LVM LV. A LUN maps that backstore into the target's namespace. The target is identified by an IQN and exposes one or more TPGs that determine which network portals it listens on. Initiators use their own IQNs and are allowed to connect when ACLs permit.

  • Backstore types: fileio, block, iblock (LVM).
  • LUNs present backstores to targets.
  • TPGs and portals control network reachability.
  • ACLs tie initiator IQNs to allowed LUNs.
Quick mapping
IQN
Globally unique name for a target or initiator used in ACLs.
TPG / Portal
Network binding for listening on IP and port 3260.
LUN
The logical disk presented to the initiator.
Common mistake

Creating an ACL for the wrong initiator IQN or adding a portal on the wrong interface will prevent discovery or login. Always verify IQNs and portal IPs match your environment.

screens.title: Creating a backstore and target with targetcli
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough shows the exact sequence you use in targetcli to expose an LVM logical volume as an iSCSI backstore and publish it as a LUN. Start targetcli with root privileges. First create a block backstore that points to your logical volume; this command registers the LV as a storage object the target can map. Next create an iSCSI target and give it an IQN that adheres to the iSCSI naming format; the IQN is used by initiators to identify and connect. Then create a portal under the target's TPG so the target listens on the server's IP and port 3260. After that, create a LUN by mapping the backstore into the target namespace. Finally, add an ACL entry with the initiator's IQN to restrict access. Save the configuration so your changes persist. A common oversight is forgetting saveconfig or failing to enable the target service. The concrete commands shown in the visual are safe to run when you replace example names and IPs with your environment values. keyIdea.text: targetcli: create backstore, create target with IQN, add portal, create LUN, create ACL, saveconfig.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Create backstore & target
Command sequence

Run targetcli and execute these commands, replacing names and IPs with your environment values.

sudo targetcli
/> /backstores/block create name=iscsi_disk0 dev=/dev/vg_iscsi/lv_iscsi_data
/> /iscsi create iqn.2023-11.com.example:storage.target0
/> /iscsi/iqn.2023-11.com.example:storage.target0/tpg1/portals create 192.168.1.100 3260
/> /iscsi/iqn.2023-11.com.example:storage.target0/tpg1/luns create /backstores/block/iscsi_disk0
/> /iscsi/iqn.2023-11.com.example:storage.target0/tpg1/acls create iqn.2023-11.com.example:client.initiator0
/> saveconfig
/> exit
Why create backstore first
The backstore is the concrete storage object mapped by LUNs; LUNs cannot exist without a backstore.
Remember to save
Without saveconfig changes may be lost after a reboot; enable the target service for persistence.
Example values

The example uses an LVM LV at /dev/vg_iscsi/lv_iscsi_data and server IP 192.168.1.100. Replace with your LV path and server IP.

Common mistake

Adding an ACL for an initiator IQN that doesn't match the initiator's /etc/iscsi/initiatorname.iscsi will prevent login. Verify the exact IQN string.

keyIdea.text: Install open-iscsi, enable services, discover targets with iscsiadm, login to create a local block device, then format and mount.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Initiator discovery & login
Commands
sudo apt install -y open-iscsi
sudo systemctl enable --now iscsid iscsi
cat /etc/iscsi/initiatorname.iscsi
sudo iscsiadm -m discovery -t sendtargets -p 192.168.1.100
sudo iscsiadm -m node -T iqn.2023-11.com.example:storage.target0 -p 192.168.1.100 --login
lsblk
sudo fdisk -l
  • Install the correct package for your distribution and enable both iscsid and iscsi services.
  • Discovery lists IQNs; login establishes the session and creates a block device on the initiator.
  • Use lsblk or fdisk to verify the new device and proceed to partition and format it.
Example verification

After login, look for a new /dev/sdX entry. Use fdisk to create a partition, then mkfs.ext4 to format it and mount to a directory to test read/write.

Common mistake

Discovery returns nothing if the target's firewall blocks port 3260 or the target is not listening on the expected IP. Use ping and telnet to test basic connectivity before deeper troubleshooting.

screens.title: Backstore types and when to use them
screens.narratorSegment: Backstores are the concrete storage objects you expose via LIO. The common types are fileio, block, and iblock. A fileio backstore is a file on the host filesystem that targetcli presents as a LUN; it is easy to create for testing but can perform poorly under heavy input and output because it goes through the host filesystem layer. A block backstore maps a raw block device directly, reducing layers and generally improving throughput. An iblock backstore typically points to an LVM logical volume, combining the advantages of raw block access with LVM features like snapshots and flexible resizing. Choose fileio for labs and quick proofs of concept, block or iblock for production where predictable input and output and reliability matter. One misconception is thinking a fileio backstore is equivalently performant to a raw LV; in practice the extra filesystem overhead on the target can cause higher latency. The takeaway: prefer LVM logical volumes or raw block devices for production iSCSI targets and reserve fileio for simple testing or temporary exports. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Backstore types
Backstore types

fileio, block, iblock

Each backstore type has predictable trade-offs. Fileio is simple but goes through the server filesystem. Block and iblock present raw devices, offering lower latency and better throughput. iblock tied to LVM lets you use snapshot and resizing workflows on the target.

  • fileio: fast to create, not optimal for heavy I/O.
  • block: maps a raw device, better performance.
  • iblock: LVM logical volume, production-friendly and flexible.
Example choice

For a production VM datastore, create an LVM LV and use iblock to back the LUN so you can take snapshots and resize without moving files around.

Performance note

Raw block and LVM-based backstores minimize extra file system overhead and are the recommended default for production LUNs.

Check your understanding

If you need snapshot capability on the target side and good performance, which backstore type is the best fit? The answer is iblock with an LVM LV because it supports snapshots and performs like a raw device.

screens.title: Enabling CHAP authentication and ACLs
screens.narratorSegment: Securing iSCSI with CHAP prevents unauthorized initiators from attaching to LUNs. CHAP uses a challenge and response; mutual CHAP requires both sides to authenticate each other. On the target, CHAP credentials are set per ACL entry within targetcli by setting auth options and providing user_id and password. Target side (targetcli)
/> /iscsi/iqn.2023-11.com.example:storage.target0/tpg1/acls/iqn.2023-11.com.example:client.initiator0 set auth=chap-mutual user_id=myuser password=mypass

Initiator side
# /etc/iscsi/iscsid.conf
node.session.auth.username = myuser
node.session.auth.password = mypass
Add the credentials to the initiator config and restart iscsid. For mutual CHAP you will need both sides to have complementary settings.
Firewall guidance

Restrict access to TCP port 3260 to trusted initiator IPs using ufw or firewalld. Even with CHAP, network isolation reduces attack surface.

Mismatched usernames or passwords between target and initiator will yield authentication failures. Copy carefully and restart services after edits.

screens.title: Post-login: partitioning, formatting, and mounting the LUN
screens.narratorSegment: Once an iSCSI session is established and the LUN appears as a block device on the initiator, you must prepare it like any local disk. First, identify the device name with lsblk. Then create a partition table and partition using fdisk or parted. After partition creation, format the partition with a filesystem such as ext4 using mkfs. ext4, and create a mount point directory. Mount the filesystem and verify read/write with standard utilities such as df -h and touch to create a test file. If you need the mount to persist across reboots, add an entry to /etc/fstab and use the _netdev option to ensure the network device is available before mounting at boot. A common misconception is expecting the device name to remain constant; it may change, so prefer using UUIDs in fstab or by device-mapper multipath. The takeaway is treat remote LUNs as you would local block devices but plan for network dependencies and persistence across reboots. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Prepare and mount LUN
Typical workflow
lsblk
sudo fdisk /dev/sdb    # create a partition
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdb1
sudo mkdir /mnt/iscsi_data
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/iscsi_data
df -h /mnt/iscsi_data
# Optional fstab entry:
# /dev/sdb1 /mnt/iscsi_data ext4 _netdev 0 0
Use UUIDs or device-mapper paths to avoid problems when device identifiers change after reboots. The _netdev mount option prevents mount attempts before the network and iSCSI session are available.
Verification

After mounting, run df -h and create a file to verify persistence. If the mount fails at boot, check that iscsid and iscsi services are enabled and that the session is logged in.

Misconception

Don't assume the LUN is safe to share between multiple systems unless you are using a clustered filesystem that supports shared block devices.

screens.title: iSCSI vs NFS: block vs file level access
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing iSCSI and NFS clarifies which storage approach fits your workload. iSCSI delivers block-level access: the initiator receives a raw block device and governs the filesystem and partitions. This is ideal for virtual machine disks and databases where performance and direct control matter. NFS provides file-level access where the server's filesystem mediates reads and writes; it is simple to share files across hosts and often suffices for home directories, shared datasets, or application artifacts. A concrete contrast: with NFS multiple clients can safely access distinct files within a shared namespace, but with iSCSI multiple hosts must not mount the same block device with independent filesystems or risk corruption unless a cluster-aware filesystem is in place. Another difference is performance: block-level operations can reduce protocol overhead and allow SAN-like features and multipathing. A common misconception is that iSCSI always outperforms NFS; performance depends on network design, backstore speed, and workload characteristics. Choose iSCSI when you need raw block semantics and consider NFS when file sharing and simplicity are the priority. iSCSI vs NFS: block vs file level access means use iscsi for raw block access and workloads requiring san semantics; use nfs when file sharing and simplicity are priorities.. In practical terms, when to prefer iscsi and when file protocols are sufficient. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › iSCSI vs NFS
iSCSI (block)
  • Provides a raw block device to the initiator.
  • Best for VM disks, databases, and SAN-like features.
  • Requires careful access control and planning for shared mounts.
NFS (file)
  • Exposes a shared filesystem namespace to clients.
  • Good for home directories and shared datasets where file-level locks are sufficient.
  • Simpler to share concurrently across many hosts without clustered filesystems.
Side-by-side example
VM disk on iSCSI
The hypervisor mounts the LUN and manages a VM filesystem directly for better I/O control.
VM disk on NFS
Virtual disk files on NFS are simpler to share but may add protocol overhead and limit some hypervisor features.
Learner check

If two hosts must access the same raw disk simultaneously, what must you ensure? Use a cluster-aware filesystem or coordination layer to avoid corruption.

screens.title: Performance considerations and tuning
screens.narratorSegment: Performance for iSCSI is primarily influenced by network bandwidth and latency and by the storage performance of the backstore on the target. Use a dedicated network for iSCSI traffic — ideally a separate physical interface or VLAN — to avoid noisy neighbor issues. Gigabit Ethernet is commonly used, but 10 gigabit reduces contention and latency for demanding workloads. Jumbo frames may improve throughput by reducing per-packet overhead, but both ends of the path must support and be configured for the same MTU. The backstore matters: SSDs and RAID controllers provide much better IOPS than single spinning disks. For resiliency and performance, consider multipathing when you have redundant network paths or HBAs. A common mistake is assuming network bandwidth alone determines performance; slow disks or a misconfigured filesystem on the target can bottleneck throughput. Measure at each layer: ping and telnet for network, iostat or sar for storage, and test read/write performance after mounting the LUN so you can identify where to optimize next. Performance considerations and tuning means tune both network and target backstore: dedicated network, matching mtus for jumbo frames, fast storage, and multipathing when needed.. In practical terms, network, jumbo frames, nic choices, and backstore impact on throughput. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Performance

Network and storage both matter

Network
  • Use a dedicated interface or VLAN for iSCSI traffic.
  • Consider 10 Gbit for heavy workloads.
  • Configure jumbo frames consistently across the path if used.
Backstore
  • SSD and RAID configurations usually outperform single HDDs.

screens.title: Common discovery and login failures
screens.narratorSegment: When discovery fails using iscsiadm, there are a handful of common root causes to check in sequence. First, firewall rules often block port 3260 on the target. Verify the server's firewall configuration and that port 3260/tcp is allowed; test connectivity using telnet to port 3260 from the initiator. Second, the target service may not be running or the targetcli configuration might not include the portal bound to the expected IP. Check the target service status and review targetcli to confirm portals are created on the correct interface. Third, basic network connectivity or routing issues can prevent discovery; use ping to confirm reachability and ip a to check interface configuration on both sides. A useful troubleshooting sequence is: ping the target, telnet to 3260, check target service, confirm portals in targetcli, check ACLs and IQNs, and finally confirm initiator services are enabled. Knowing this ordered checklist saves time and avoids chasing misleading symptoms. Common discovery and login failures means check firewall → check target service and portals → verify basic network connectivity and routing.. Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Troubleshooting discovery
Diagnosis

Three common causes

Firewall blocking port 3260
Check ufw or firewalld on the target and allow 3260/tcp. Use telnet from the initiator to verify the port is reachable.
Target service not running or wrong portal
Verify the target service is active and the portal IP matches the interface where discovery is attempted.
Network connectivity issues
Use ping and ip a to check reachability and routing; ensure both hosts are on a network path that allows TCP 3260.
Stepwise check

Recommended order: ping target → telnet port 3260 → check target service → verify portals in targetcli → confirm ACL and IQN match → check initiator services.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn what iSCSI provides and why administrators use it. iSCSI delivers block-level storage over ordinary IP networks, allowing a remote LUN to behave like a locally attached disk. That matters because many server workloads — databases, virtual machine disks, and clustered filesystems — require raw block access for performance and control. We will focus on the Linux tooling: LIO as the kernel target framework and targetcli to build backstores, targets, portals, LUNs, and ACLs. You will also learn how to configure an initiator with iscsiadm, how CHAP authentication protects access, and what network and storage choices influence performance. A short lab demonstrates creating a 2 gigabyte logical volume, exporting it from a target, discovering and logging in from an initiator, then partitioning, formatting, and mounting the discovered disk. Common troubleshooting steps such as checking firewalls, verifying the target service, and testing basic TCP connectivity are included so you can diagnose discovery failures quickly. By the end you should understand when to choose iSCSI over file protocols and how to build a basic, secure iSCSI pair in Linux.

These objectives map to hands-on skills you need for iSCSI administration in Linux. First, you will explain iSCSI architecture: the difference between targets and initiators, and why block-level access matters. Second, you will configure a Linux server as an iSCSI target using the LIO kernel framework and targetcli, including creating backstores and publishing LUNs. Third, you will configure a Linux initiator with iscsiadm to discover, log in, and use remote block devices. Fourth, you will implement authentication and access control, including CHAP credentials and ACLs. Each objective is paired with why it matters: for example, creating proper ACLs prevents unauthorized block access, and correct initiator configuration ensures the system sees a stable block device. We emphasize hands-on commands and verification steps so you can both build and troubleshoot deployments in real environments.

This second objectives screen highlights practice steps and pitfalls. First, practice creating backstores from different storage types: files, raw block devices, and LVM logical volumes. Each backstore type behaves differently and has trade-offs in performance and snapshotting. Second, practice defining portals and TPGs so the target listens on the correct IP and port; misconfigured portals are a frequent cause of failures. Third, learn to verify that the target service is running and that you have saved the targetcli configuration so your setup persists across reboots. Fourth, practice troubleshooting discovery failures: check firewalls, verify service status, and test basic TCP connectivity to port 3260. Understanding these tasks reduces downtime and prevents configuration drift in production environments. Practical skills and considerations means hands-on practice with backstores, portals, saving config, and basic tcp troubleshooting reduces common configuration errors.. In practical terms, what to practice and common mistakes to avoid. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

iSCSI is a protocol that exposes block storage over TCP/IP so a remote device appears as a local disk. That distinction — block versus file access — is critical. With file protocols like NFS, the client operates at the file level and the server's filesystem mediates input and output. With iSCSI, the initiator receives a raw block device and can partition, format, and manage filesystems directly. This direct access benefits workloads that depend on predictable block semantics and performance, such as databases and virtual machine disks, because there is no intermediate server filesystem layer handling each file operation. A concrete example: a hypervisor connecting a VM disk to centralized storage can mount the LUN and use its own filesystem optimizations and caching, often improving throughput and enabling features like multipathing. The takeaway is to choose iSCSI when you need raw block semantics and ensure your architecture accounts for exclusive access or clustering solutions when sharing LUNs between hosts.

Understanding the components and their relationships prevents configuration mistakes. The iSCSI target is the server that exports storage; it uses backstores to represent the physical or logical devices that will be presented. The initiator is the client that connects and consumes a LUN as a block device. IQNs — iSCSI Qualified Names — uniquely identify targets and initiators and are used in ACLs. A LUN, or Logical Unit Number, maps a backstore to the target so it is presented to an initiator. A TPG, or Target Portal Group, defines the network interfaces and ports where the target listens; a portal ties a target to an IP and port combination, typically TCP 3260. For example, you might expose an LVM Logical Volume as a backstore, create a target with an IQN, add a portal binding to 192.168.1.100:3260, then create a LUN that maps the LV so that an initiator with a permitted IQN can attach. A common error is mismatched IQNs in ACLs or forgetting to create the portal on the correct interface. The core idea is that backstores become LUNs, which targets expose through portals and protect with ACLs identified by IQN.

Backstores are the concrete storage objects you expose via LIO. The common types are fileio, block, and iblock. A fileio backstore is a file on the host filesystem that targetcli presents as a LUN; it is easy to create for testing but can perform poorly under heavy input and output because it goes through the host filesystem layer. A block backstore maps a raw block device directly, reducing layers and generally improving throughput. An iblock backstore typically points to an LVM logical volume, combining the advantages of raw block access with LVM features like snapshots and flexible resizing. Choose fileio for labs and quick proofs of concept, block or iblock for production where predictable input and output and reliability matter. One misconception is thinking a fileio backstore is equivalently performant to a raw LV; in practice the extra filesystem overhead on the target can cause higher latency. The takeaway: prefer LVM logical volumes or raw block devices for production iSCSI targets and reserve fileio for simple testing or temporary exports. Comparing iSCSI and NFS clarifies which storage approach fits your workload. iSCSI delivers block-level access: the initiator receives a raw block device and governs the filesystem and partitions. This is ideal for virtual machine disks and databases where performance and direct control matter. NFS provides file-level access where the server's filesystem mediates reads and writes; it is simple to share files across hosts and often suffices for home directories, shared datasets, or application artifacts. A concrete contrast: with NFS multiple clients can safely access distinct files within a shared namespace, but with iSCSI multiple hosts must not mount the same block device with independent filesystems or risk corruption unless a cluster-aware filesystem is in place. Another difference is performance: block-level operations can reduce protocol overhead and allow SAN-like features and multipathing. A common misconception is that iSCSI always outperforms NFS; performance depends on network design, backstore speed, and workload characteristics. Performance for iSCSI is primarily influenced by network bandwidth and latency and by the storage performance of the backstore on the target. Use a dedicated network for iSCSI traffic — ideally a separate physical interface or VLAN — to avoid noisy neighbor issues. Gigabit Ethernet is commonly used, but 10 gigabit reduces contention and latency for demanding workloads. Jumbo frames may improve throughput by reducing per-packet overhead, but both ends of the path must support and be configured for the same MTU. The backstore matters: SSDs and RAID controllers provide much better IOPS than single spinning disks. For resiliency and performance, consider multipathing when you have redundant network paths or HBAs. A common mistake is assuming network bandwidth alone determines performance; slow disks or a misconfigured filesystem on the target can bottleneck throughput. When discovery fails using iscsiadm, there are a handful of common root causes to check in sequence. First, firewall rules often block port 3260 on the target. Verify the server's firewall configuration and that port 3260/tcp is allowed; test connectivity using telnet to port 3260 from the initiator. Second, the target service may not be running or the targetcli configuration might not include the portal bound to the expected IP. Check the target service status and review targetcli to confirm portals are created on the correct interface. Third, basic network connectivity or routing issues can prevent discovery; use ping to confirm reachability and ip a to check interface configuration on both sides. A useful troubleshooting sequence is: ping the target, telnet to 3260, check target service, confirm portals in targetcli, check ACLs and IQNs, and finally confirm initiator services are enabled.
